gui.distantstock.manual.p1: First place and enable an unlocked Stock Link on the warehouse server. Distant Stock publishes it to every connected server. Players can open an untuned requester anywhere and select an open network without visiting the warehouse. Use a joined requester on a telegraph to copy it there.
gui.distantstock.manual.p2: The warehouse can use the pale-blue Distant Packager. It keeps Create packing logic and produces Distant Parcels. Face the dock cabin toward the operator and leave the sides free for a belt or hopper. An import dock matches address only (blank = *). A parcel in the bay means the slots are occupied.
gui.distantstock.manual.p3: Players never type an IP. OP runs /distantstock, or sneak-clicks a monitor. Pick Host (warehouse) or Client (outer), fill self id, listen, peer, password. Save writes this server's config/distantstock-common.toml and restarts the listener. Same password on every side.
gui.distantstock.manual.p4: One warehouse, many survival servers. Orders carry from=self.id. After packing, the warehouse POSTs the package only to that origin. Outer servers pull /stock from the host only. Outer servers do not act as warehouses for each other.
gui.distantstock.manual.p5: Goggles show live data only: dock mode, short freq or address, UP/DOWN, slots or backlog. Desk: freq, address, catalog size. Monitor: TPS and queue. The tutorial lives in this book. Set giveManual=false to stop handing one out on first join.

block.distantstock.dock.desc: Full casing, pipes into the sides and a fallback face underneath that needs a chute. Lamp: off = offline, green = standby, cyan blinking = dispatching, orange blinking = fallback blocked, red = fault.
block.distantstock.tower_casing.desc: Decorative casing with connected textures on all six faces. A redstone signal turns the centre of linked casings into a see-through window; the propagation range is configurable.
block.distantstock.tower_core.desc: The centre of the tower’s 3x3 base, driven by rotation from below. Stack couplers on top of it and cap them with an ether resonator to raise a tower.
block.distantstock.tower_coupler.desc: A segment of the mast. The taller the stack, the higher the tier — and the more distant devices and chunks it carries.
block.distantstock.ether_resonator.desc: The cap. Turning arms mean the tower is running; it only starts once the tower is complete.
block.distantstock.gauge.desc: Floor stock desk. Use a joined requester to write its network.
block.distantstock.monitor.desc: Wall dashboard: local/peer TPS and link pressure. OP sneak-click opens link setup.
block.distantstock.remote_packager.desc: A pale-blue Create packager variant. It keeps addresses and contents while producing Distant Parcels.

distantstock.ponder.distant_export.text_: Every parcel begins in storage. Set a Distant Packager against the chest and turn it to face the line: when an order arrives it seals the goods into a Distant Parcel and hands it on by itself.
This is the dock, the one door the goods leave through. It holds a single parcel at a time, so everything upstream of it is a queue rather than a buffer.
A belt joins the two. Keep the run flat and let its last block point into the dock: the parcel is handed over as it arrives, with nobody standing there to feed it in.
With a parcel aboard, the lift rises and passes it through the ether surface. The two stock networks stay separate throughout: only the sealed parcel crosses between them.
The underside is the fallback face, and it cannot be seen from here. Leave it clear, or a parcel that comes back will have nowhere to go.
distantstock.ponder.distant_import.text_: On the server that receives, the dock is given a delivery address instead of a destination. Sneak-click it with a Requester to write one in.

A hopper gathers what the dock releases from underneath, and the belt carries it on to storage. The same two blocks serve the other direction as well, which is why the fallback face is worth keeping clear.
The far end is an ordinary chest. Nothing here knows what the goods cost on the other server, and nothing there knows what became of them here; the parcel is the only thing that travelled.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tune.text_1: The Request Desk is the Requester in furniture form. It carries the same network and the same address, so an order written here is an order the packing line can read.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tune.text_2: Right-click a dock with a tuned Requester to make it a destination for goods, and sneak-click to give it a delivery address. The desk reports what it did in the line above your hotbar.
distantstock.ponder.distant_tune.text_3: The desk is a place to stand and write, not a machine on the goods path. Give it its own spot beside the line, where the belt will not have to route around it later.
distantstock.ponder.distant_status.text_: The glass lid is the link light. It stays dull while the far side is out of reach, and lights when the two ends find each other, so a glance from across the room is enough to tell whether the line is up.
The wall monitor keeps a longer record: which links are up, how much each side is carrying, and the coordinates of any link that has dropped.
Clearing a fault is deliberate. A dock that has given up waits at red until someone right-clicks it, so a failure cannot be mistaken for an idle machine and quietly forgotten.

The lamp, in order of how much it wants your attention: dark for no network, green for standing by, cyan for a parcel on its way up, orange for cargo waiting on a blocked fallback face, and red for a fault.

Everything the far server will not accept leaves through the underside and waits there. Give it a container or a belt to fall into; with nothing below, the dock holds the cargo and blinks orange until you make room.
